headline: Pappas leads $3 billion push for emergency home-heating aid
dek: The New Hampshire congressman is asking House appropriators to add money to LIHEAP as lawmakers warn that rising energy costs could leave more eligible households without help this winter.
body: Rep. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire is leading a new congressional request for $3 billion in emergency funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, a proposal aimed at helping households manage heating and cooling bills during the 2027 fiscal year. Pappas’s office said Oct. 15 that 73 members signed the request to the House Appropriations Committee. The request is not an enacted appropriation, so it does not yet create new benefits or change what New Hampshire residents can receive.

The lawmakers’ [letter to appropriations leaders](https://pappas.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/pappas-evo.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/10.14.2026-letter-to-appropriators-requesting-liheap-supplemental-64.pdf), dated Oct. 14, says heating oil prices have risen 60% since February and argues that the program’s $4 billion allocation in the prior fiscal year would not meet this year’s need. Pappas’s [official announcement](https://pappas.house.gov/media/press-releases/pappas-leads-bipartisan-call-to-increase-home-heating-assistance-funding) attributes those figures to the letter. The proposal would add emergency money; it would not itself guarantee a payment to any applicant or establish a new eligibility rule.

LIHEAP is the federal program that helps low-income households pay for home energy. Pappas’s office says the program reaches nearly 6 million households nationally, including nearly 30,000 in New Hampshire, citing federal program data. The same release says five of six households that qualify receive no assistance because funding is limited. That statistic is an estimate presented by the lawmakers, not a new count of New Hampshire applicants, and it describes the program’s national reach rather than the number of Granite State households currently waiting for aid.

The funding request arrives as New Hampshire community-action agencies are already preparing for higher demand. [New Hampshire Public Radio](https://www.nhpr.org/business/2026-10-12/high-fuel-costs-nh-newhampshire-heating-assistance) reported that agencies were seeing more first-time applicants while the state’s heating-oil benchmark approached $6 per gallon and seasonal benefits were not scheduled for release until Dec. 1. That state-level pressure is related to, but separate from, the federal request: New Hampshire’s Fuel Assistance Program distributes LIHEAP support locally, while Congress controls the federal funding pool behind it.

The letter also points to broader household-budget strain. It cites estimates that about one in six U.S. households are behind on utility bills and that low- and moderate-income households can spend as much as 10% of their income on energy. Those figures come from sources listed in the lawmakers’ letter, including the National Energy Assistance Directors Association and other policy organizations. They are national estimates and should not be read as a current survey of New Hampshire residents.

Pappas has made LIHEAP a recurring part of his energy-cost agenda. His office says he led a separate September request urging the Department of Health and Human Services to distribute the program’s funds to states by Nov. 1, and he recently introduced the American Homes First Act, which would redirect $1 billion to LIHEAP. Earlier appeals and a bill are steps in the debate, not evidence that Congress has approved either the $3 billion supplemental request or the proposed $1 billion transfer.

Independent Washington coverage also identified the latest push. [Punchbowl News](https://punchbowl.news/article/house/pappas-liheap-supplemental/) reported that Pappas was seeking a $3 billion emergency supplemental for LIHEAP, describing the effort as involving more than 70 Democrats. Pappas’s office, meanwhile, characterized its signers as a bipartisan group of 73 members. The difference in description is worth noting because the official release and the independent report frame the coalition differently, even though both identify the same funding request.

The next decision belongs to congressional appropriators, who would have to include the supplemental money in legislation before it could reach the program. Until then, New Hampshire households facing winter bills should rely on the state’s existing Fuel Assistance Program and local community-action agencies for current eligibility and application information. The new request signals that lawmakers see a national funding shortfall; it does not resolve how much money will ultimately be available, when it would be distributed or whether Congress will approve it.
location: New Hampshire and the U.S. House of Representatives
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Pappas seeks $3 billion more for LIHEAP heating aid
seoDescription: Rep. Chris Pappas is leading a request for $3 billion in emergency LIHEAP funding as New Hampshire agencies prepare for higher heating-aid demand.
